questions.q: What type does TypeScript infer for const row = ["2026-09-01", "Airtime", -500];?
questions.explain: An array literal on its own is inferred as an array: any length, and every element may be any of the element types. You need an annotation, a return type, as const or a const type parameter to get a tuple.

questions.q: What does a tuple type such as [string, number] describe?
questions.explain: A tuple fixes the length and the type at each position. At runtime it is an ordinary JavaScript array.
options: An array of strings and numbers in any order and any length
An array with exactly two elements: a string at index 0 and a number at index 1
A special runtime structure that cannot be changed

questions.q: For const t: [string, string, number] = ["ACC-1", "ACC-2", 500];, what is the type of t.length?
questions.explain: A tuple knows its length, so length has the literal type 3. For a tuple with optional elements it becomes a union, such as 2 | 3.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The tuple return gives two values, and destructuring names them in order: the first element is the share, the second the leftover kobo that cannot be split evenly.

questions.q: What do the labels in [from: string, to: string, kobo: number] change?
questions.explain: [from: string] and [string] are the same type. Labels are for people reading the code and hovering in the editor.
options: They make the tuple an object with from, to and kobo properties
They force callers to destructure with exactly those names
Nothing about the type; they document the positions in editors and error messages

questions.q: What happens with const [a, b, c] = pair; when pair is typed [number, number]?
questions.explain: TypeScript knows which indexes exist in a tuple, so destructuring or reading past the end is caught before the code runs.
options: Compile error TS2493: the tuple of length 2 has no element at index 2

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An optional element that is left out is simply missing, so destructuring gives undefined and ?? prints -. The arrays have 2 and 3 elements; the type of length is 2 | 3.

questions.q: Which tuple type is invalid?
questions.explain: A required element cannot follow an optional one, because TypeScript could not tell which position a value belongs to. Optional elements go at the end.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The rest element means zero or more numbers after the branch. A rest pattern in destructuring always gives an array, empty for "Wuse", and reduce with a start value of 0 handles the empty case.

questions.q: What does [...path: string[], kobo: number] describe?
questions.explain: A rest element can appear at the start, in the middle or at the end, as long as there is only one. Here it collects the leading strings, and the final position is always a number.
options: Exactly one string followed by one number
Any number of strings, then exactly one number at the end
A number followed by any number of strings
It is invalid: rest elements must come last

questions.q: This compiles. What does it print?
questions.explain: A tuple is a real array, and plain tuple types still allow push. The type keeps saying "two elements" while the array has three. A readonly tuple would refuse the push.
options: A TypeError, because tuples cannot grow

questions.q: Which of these compiles on const pair: readonly [string, number] = ["USD", 1550];?
questions.explain: A readonly tuple removes every method that changes the array, and assignment to elements. toSorted returns a new array and leaves the original alone, so it is allowed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: b - a sorts from largest to smallest. toSorted returns a new array, so topUps is unchanged and its first element is still 5000.

questions.q: Why is a parameter typed readonly [string, number] friendlier than [string, number]?
questions.explain: A mutable tuple can be passed where a readonly one is expected, but not the other way round. readonly on inputs is both more flexible and a promise.
options: It accepts both mutable and readonly tuples, and promises the function will not change the caller's array
It converts the argument into a frozen copy

questions.q: What type does const pair = ["NGN", 1] as const; have?
questions.explain: as const makes the literal a readonly tuple of literal types: the most precise type possible, which is often more precise than you need for values that are not constants.

questions.q: function rate(c: string) { return [c, 1550]; } has no return type. What do callers get?
questions.explain: The returned literal is inferred as an array. Adding the return type [currency: string, rate: number] turns it into a tuple, and every caller keeps the positions.
options: (string | number)[], so const [code, value] = rate("USD") gives two string | number values

questions.q: What does the const in function tuple<const T extends readonly unknown[]>(...items: T): T do?
questions.explain: A const type parameter (TypeScript 5.0) asks for the narrowest inference, without the caller writing as const at every call site.
options: It makes the returned array frozen at runtime
It infers T as if the caller had written as const, so tuple("GBP", 2050) is readonly ["GBP", 2050]
It forbids calling the function more than once
It is required for every generic function that returns an array

questions.q: Why does React's useState return a tuple rather than an object like { value, setValue }?
questions.explain: Destructuring a tuple assigns by position, so names are free. An object would force every caller to rename: const { value: count, setValue: setCount } = ….
options: Tuples are faster to create than objects
With a tuple, each caller chooses its own names when destructuring: const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
Tuples are the only type TypeScript can infer from a function

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call to createState has its own value, captured by both returned functions. Setting one cart does not affect the other.

questions.q: With createState<T>(initial: T), why do you write createState<string | null>(null) for a coupon code?
questions.explain: Inference uses the initial value. null alone gives T = null. Passing the type argument says what the state will hold over its lifetime.
options: Because null is not allowed as a generic argument
Because T would be inferred as null from the argument, and setting a real code later would be a type error
Because strings must always be passed explicitly

questions.q: What is the type of results in const results = await Promise.all([loadUser(), loadBalance()]), where the two functions return Promise<User> and Promise<number>?
questions.explain: Promise.all maps a tuple of promises to a tuple of their results, so each position keeps its own type. await unwraps the outer promise.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Object.entries returns an array of [key, value] pairs, typed [string, number][]. The first pair is printed as a two-element array.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Parameters<typeof transfer> is the tuple [from: string, to: string, kobo: number]. Spreading a tuple into the call passes each element as a separate argument, checked by position.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The union of tuples narrows on the null element even after destructuring, so amount * 100 compiles in the success branch. The explicit empty-string check matters: Number("") is 0, not NaN.

questions.q: Why does [error: string, row: null] | [error: null, row: Row] narrow after if (error !== null) return;?
questions.explain: A unit type like null (or a literal) in the same position of each member lets TypeScript tell the members apart, exactly like a kind property in a discriminated union.
options: Because TypeScript narrows every array after a null check
Because the first element is null in one member and string in the other, so it works as a discriminant, even across destructuring
It does not narrow; row stays Row | null

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A trailing comma produces an empty last cell, so there are three cells. Number("") is 0, which is why a parser must reject an empty amount explicitly instead of trusting Number.isFinite.

questions.q: A client sends {"rate": ["USD", 1550]}. What type does JSON.parse give rate, and what should you do?
questions.explain: JSON has arrays, not tuples, and JSON.parse returns any. A tuple from outside is outside data like any other, so its length and every position must be checked.
options: No tuple type at all (any); check that it is an array of length 2 with a string and a number before using it

questions.q: Which value is the best fit for a tuple rather than an object?
questions.explain: Tuples suit short, obvious groups that callers take apart at once and name themselves. Records with many fields, public JSON and optional settings are clearer as objects with named properties.
options: A customer with name, e-mail, phone, BVN and date of birth
An API response field sent to many different clients
A function that returns [getter, setter], destructured immediately by each caller
A configuration with ten optional settings

questions.q: After const [date, description, amount, reference] = line.split(",");, what type does TypeScript give reference with default strict settings?
questions.explain: split returns string[], and without noUncheckedIndexedAccess, every element read from an array is typed as the element type. That option adds | undefined so you cannot forget the check.
options: string, even though a three-column line leaves it undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A Map is built from [key, value] tuples and spreads back into them. Setting an existing key replaces the value, so there are still two entries.

questions.q: Finish range so it returns a readonly tuple [min, max] for a non-empty list, and null for an empty one.
questions.explain: The return type turns the array literal into a tuple. The empty case is part of the type, so the caller must check for null before destructuring.

questions.q: Write useToggle(initial) returning a readonly tuple [isOn, toggle] of two functions that share one boolean.
questions.explain: Keep the state in a let inside the function. Both returned functions close over it, so a toggle is visible through the getter.

questions.q: Finish parseRow: split on commas and trim. Exactly three cells, a date like 2026-09-01 and a finite, non-empty amount give [null, [date, description, kobo]] (kobo = naira × 100, rounded). Anything else gives ["invalid", null].
questions.explain: Every failure returns the error tuple, so the caller's destructured error === null check narrows row to a Row. The empty amount must be refused explicitly, because Number("") is 0.

questions.q: The rate tuple is mutated with push. Make the type readonly and, instead of pushing, create a new tuple next with the updated rate 1600.
questions.explain: A readonly tuple cannot grow or change, so "updating" it means building a new tuple. The old value stays intact, which also makes the change easy to see and test.

questions.q: Type the queue with Parameters<typeof transfer> and run every queued call by spreading the saved arguments.
questions.explain: Without the annotation, queued is (string | number)[][] and transfer(...args) does not compile. With the parameter tuple type, each saved call is checked by position, and the spread passes the elements as separate arguments.

questions.q: Load the user and the balance at the same time with Promise.all, destructure the resulting tuple, and print NAME: ₦NAIRA (the balance is in kobo).
questions.explain: Promise.all on a tuple of promises returns a tuple of results, so user is { name: string } and kobo is number, and both loads run at once.

questions.q: Finish the loop: print LABEL: KOBO, and add (free for PLAN) only when the optional third element is present.
questions.explain: Destructuring an optional element gives string | undefined, so it must be narrowed before use, exactly like an optional property.

questions.q: Use Object.entries and destructure each [account, kobo] pair to print only the accounts with a positive balance, as ACCOUNT KOBO.
questions.explain: Object.entries returns [string, number][], an array of pairs, so each loop variable can be destructured into two named values with their own types.
